newsitem.title: USA: U.S. bank bill's prospects clouded by a close vote.
newsitem.headline: U.S. bank bill's prospects clouded by a close vote.

text.p: The House Banking Committee on Friday approved sweeping legislation to overhaul U.S. banking laws, but the bill's narrow two-vote margin of victory may not be enough to keep the legislation moving forward.

After months of drafting and four days of intense debate, the committee voted 28 to 26 to approve the measure, which would tear down the Depression-era barriers separating banking from other financial services.
Opposition to the bill was bipartisan, as 12 Republicans joined 14 Democrats voting "nay." Supporters counted 18 Republicans and 10 Democrats among their ranks.
"This bill is in real trouble," said industry analyst Bert Ely, president of Ely & Co. "This is an incredibly weak vote."
But the committee's chairman, Jim Leach, Republican of Iowa, argued the vote simply reflected the balanced nature of the legislation.
"It says these are extremely sensitive issues with extremely great balancing differences," Leach told reporters after the vote.
Both the banking and insurance industries had serious problems with parts of the bill, although neither was seen actively opposing the bill in the banking committee.

Vocal opponents of the bill included consumer groups, some savings and loan groups and small bankers. Opposition hardened after the committee agreed on Tuesday and Wednesday to amendments permitting banks to own or be owned by non-financial, commercial companies. Thrifts turned against the measure after an amendment failed on Thursday to preserve the industry's distinct federal charter.
Ranking Democrat Henry Gonzalez, who strongly opposed mixing banking and commerce and eliminating thrifts, voted against the bill.
"This bill is a great disappointment," he said. "Instead of making reasonable and needed changes, it makes radical and needless change."

Chairman Leach also opposed mixing banking and commerce, but voted for the bill in the end. He told reporters the provision might be weakened if the bill moves to the House floor. "It will be a close call on the House floor," he said.

The legislation next goes to the House Commerce Committee for further consideration. That committee is likely to enhance sections of the bill giving state insurance regulators power over national banks selling insurance, a move sure to anger the banking industry.

The bill passed by the banking committee gives federal regulators the authority to overrule state insurance regulation of banks in some instances. Most attempts to amend the bill to weaken or limit federal preemption authority failed, although an amendment to prohibit banks from selling title insurance was adopted.
Banks were upset by the title insurance ban and a mandate that banks must provide low-cost "lifeline" bank accounts.

For more than a decade, Congress has been considering scrapping the 1933 Glass-Steagall Act, which separates banking from securities, but the efforts have always been blocked when the various financial service industries failed to reach a consensus. The banking committee has approved legislation on three previous occassions.
